title: Date and Time Portability Across DBMS Products
learningObjectives: Describe SQLite's common date/time storage representations.
Use SQLite date(), strftime() and julianday() for basic date calculations.
Recognize native date/time types in MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL.
Explain why time-zone context matters when storing instants.
Translate date arithmetic only after checking the target DBMS function and type semantics.

understand.concept: Date and time storage and functions differ across database products. SQLite has no dedicated date/time storage class and commonly uses ISO-8601 TEXT, Julian day REAL or Unix timestamp INTEGER values. Other DBMS products provide native date/time types and different date arithmetic functions.
understand.whyItMatters: Consistent date/time handling is essential for reporting, time zones, scheduling and data exchange.
understand.analogy: SQL portability is like translating a precise instruction into several product dialects: the intent stays the same, but the exact words and rules can differ.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model type systems, function return types, time-zone rules, optimizer behaviour or transaction semantics.

explain.narrative:
## SQLite date/time representation
SQLite date/time values are commonly stored as ISO-8601 text, Julian day numbers or Unix timestamps. Built-in functions include date(), time(), datetime(), julianday(), unixepoch() and strftime().

## Server database differences
MySQL has DATE, TIME, DATETIME and TIMESTAMP types and functions such as DATE_ADD and NOW. SQL Server has DATE, DATETIME2 and functions such as DATEADD and GETDATE. PostgreSQL has timestamp with/without time zone and interval arithmetic.

## Time-zone discipline
Store a clearly defined instant, commonly normalized to UTC, and preserve the original zone when business rules require it. Do not assume that a date string without a zone identifies a universal instant.

### Date, time and time-zone semantics
A DATE represents a calendar date; a local timestamp represents wall-clock time in a chosen zone; a UTC instant represents a point on the global timeline. Do not store a local timestamp as if it were UTC. Daylight-saving transitions and zone changes can make local-time arithmetic nontrivial.

### Product-specific APIs
SQLite uses date(), datetime(), julianday(), unixepoch() and strftime(); MySQL provides DATE_ADD and NOW(); SQL Server provides DATEADD and GETDATE(); PostgreSQL supports timestamp types and interval arithmetic. Verify return types, precision and time-zone conversions in the target engine.

examples.title: Create an event date table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE dialect16_dates (event_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, event_name TEXT NOT NULL, event_date TEXT NOT NULL);
examples.explanation: Creates an events table with ISO-formatted date text. SQLite has no dedicated DATE storage class; the chosen text representation is a convention that must be applied consistently.

examples.title: Insert ISO-8601 date values
examples.explanation: Inserts two date-only values in YYYY-MM-DD format. This representation sorts chronologically as text when every value follows the same fixed-width ISO format.

examples.title: Extract a year with SQLite strftime
examples.code: SELECT event_name, strftime('%Y', event_date) AS event_year FROM dialect16_dates ORDER BY event_id;
examples.explanation: Uses SQLite strftime('%Y', ...) to extract the year component from each date. The function and format tokens are SQLite-specific and should not be copied unchanged into another DBMS.

examples.title: Add days using SQLite date()
examples.explanation: Adds seven calendar days using SQLite's date() modifier syntax. The result is 2026-11-29; other engines use different date arithmetic functions or interval expressions.

examples.title: Calculate a day difference
examples.explanation: Subtracts Julian day values to calculate the number of days between two dates. The difference is 13 days; Julian day arithmetic is useful for elapsed-day calculations but does not replace time-zone-aware instant arithmetic.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and calculate the difference between the two event dates. Identify the SQLite functions used.
practise.independentTask: Design a date/time column strategy for an application that stores event instants from multiple time zones. Compare SQLite, MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL representations.
hints: SQLite commonly stores dates as ISO-8601 text, Julian day numbers or Unix timestamps.
Use strftime() for formatted date parts in SQLite.
MySQL DATE_ADD and SQL Server DATEADD are product-specific functions.
PostgreSQL supports interval arithmetic and timestamp types.
Define whether a value is a local date, local time or UTC instant.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes SQLite date/time storage?
options: It commonly uses TEXT, REAL or INTEGER representations
It has one mandatory native TIMESTAMP storage class
It stores every date as a BLOB
questions.answer: It commonly uses TEXT, REAL or INTEGER representations
questions.explanation: SQLite date/time values can be stored in several representations.

questions.prompt: Which SQLite function formats date parts?
questions.explanation: strftime() formats date/time values in SQLite.

questions.prompt: Which function is commonly used by SQL Server to add date parts?
questions.explanation: SQL Server uses DATEADD for date arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Why should time-zone context be preserved?
options: A local timestamp without a zone may not identify a unique instant
It makes all dates sort alphabetically
It converts dates into primary keys
questions.answer: A local timestamp without a zone may not identify a unique instant
questions.explanation: Time-zone information is needed to interpret instants correctly.

questions.prompt: Which approach is safest for cross-system date arithmetic?
options: Check the target DBMS types, functions and time-zone semantics
Assume every product uses the same function names
Store all dates as arbitrary text with no format
questions.answer: Check the target DBMS types, functions and time-zone semantics
questions.explanation: Date/time portability requires checking product-specific semantics.
